subject: physics-hl
title: When a mean-speed rule works
stem: A particle moves along a line with initial velocity $u$ and final velocity $v$. Which condition guarantees that its displacement over time $t$ is $(u+v)t/2$?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A1 validity of acceleration models. Skill focus: uniform acceleration condition. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: B

subject: physics-hl
title: A delayed catch
stem: A runner passes a stationary cyclist at $6.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The cyclist waits $2.0\,\mathrm{s}$ and then accelerates from rest at $2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. How long after the cyclist starts does the cyclist catch the runner?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A1 relative position and interception. Skill focus: two-body interception. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

steps.text: Option B. If $\tau$ starts with the cyclist, $x_C=\tau^2$ and $x_R=6(\tau+2)$. Thus $\tau^2-6\tau-12=0$, whose positive root is $3+\sqrt{21}=7.58\,\mathrm{s}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Equal projectile ranges
stem: Two projectiles leave and land at the same level with equal initial speed, at angles $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ above horizontal. Drag is negligible. Which statement is correct?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A1 angled projectile components and range. Skill focus: range versus flight time. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

options.label: A
options.text: Their ranges are equal; the $60^\circ$ flight lasts $\sqrt3$ times as long.

options.label: B
options.text: The $60^\circ$ range is $\sqrt3$ times as large; times are equal.

options.label: C
options.text: Their ranges and flight times are equal.

options.label: D
options.text: The $30^\circ$ range is twice as large; its flight lasts twice as long.

steps.text: Option A. $R=u^2\sin2\theta/g$ is equal for complementary angles. $T=2u\sin\theta/g$, so $T_{60}/T_{30}=\sin60^\circ/\sin30^\circ=\sqrt3$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Uniform circular motion
stem: A bead moves at constant speed around a horizontal circle. Which statement describes its acceleration?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A2 uniform circular force relations. Skill focus: centripetal acceleration direction. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: A
options.text: It points away from the centre.

options.label: B
options.text: It points towards the centre and is nonzero.

options.label: C
options.text: It is zero because speed is constant.

steps.text: Option B. Velocity changes direction even though its magnitude is constant. The acceleration points towards the centre, with magnitude $v^2/r$.

steps.text: Option A. At the limiting condition $T=0$. Weight alone supplies inward force: $mg=mv^2/r$, so $v=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt8=2.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Steady power acceleration
stem: A motor supplies constant useful power to a vehicle on a level frictionless road. As the vehicle’s speed increases, what happens to the driving force and acceleration?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A3 constant power motion. Skill focus: constant power force. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

steps.text: Option B. $P=Fv$ gives $F=P/v$. With constant mass, $a=F/m=P/(mv)$, so both decrease as speed increases.

subject: physics-hl
title: Raising water
stem: A pump raises $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water each second through $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$. Its efficiency is $80\%$. Use $g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. What input power is required?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A3 work and power in lifting. Skill focus: lifting useful power. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

steps.text: Option A. Useful power is $\dot mgh=4.0(10)(5.0)=200\,\mathrm{W}$. Input power is $200/0.80=250\,\mathrm{W}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Falling with resistance
stem: A ball falls at constant terminal speed. Which statement is correct over a downward displacement?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A3 dissipation and energy accounting. Skill focus: mechanical versus total energy. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: A
options.text: Its total mechanical energy is conserved.

options.label: B
options.text: Gravity does no work because acceleration is zero.

options.label: C
options.text: Its kinetic energy stays constant while gravitational potential energy is transferred to the surroundings.

options.label: D
options.text: Its gravitational potential energy remains constant.

steps.text: Option C. Terminal speed means constant kinetic energy. Gravity does positive work and drag does equal negative work; gravitational potential energy is dissipated.

stem: Two equal-mass vehicles are stopped by the same constant resultant braking-force magnitude. Vehicle Q begins with $1.5$ times vehicle P’s speed. Both have the same reaction time. Which statement is correct?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A3 energy constraints on motion. Skill focus: work energy braking scaling. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: A
options.text: Q has $1.5$ times the braking distance but $2.25$ times the reaction distance.

options.label: B
options.text: Q has $2.25$ times the braking distance but $1.5$ times the reaction distance.

options.label: C
options.text: Both distances for Q are $2.25$ times as large.

options.label: D
options.text: Both distances for Q are $1.5$ times as large.

steps.text: Option B. From $Fs=\tfrac12mv^2$, braking distance scales as $v^2$. Reaction distance $vt_r$ scales as $v$, giving $2.25$ and $1.5$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Power against a quadratic drag
stem: A vehicle’s only resistance at constant speed is $F_D=kv^2$, with constant $k$. Its useful driving power is increased by a factor of 8. What is the ratio of new to old steady speed?

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A3 power against resistance. Skill focus: drag power scaling. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

steps.text: Option A. At steady speed, $P=F_Dv=kv^3$, so $v\propto P^{1/3}$ and the ratio is $8^{1/3}=2$.

title: Stopping against a spring

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A3 energy constraints on motion. Skill focus: energy and circular threshold. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

subject: physics-hl
title: Downhill emergency braking
stem: A $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ vehicle starts braking at $20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ on a road descending at an angle with $\sin\theta=0.10$. The braking and resistive force totals a constant $5000\,\mathrm{N}$ uphill. Use $g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A3 energy constraints on motion. Skill focus: braking energy against gravity. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

parts.label: b

The downhill conversion of gravitational potential energy increases the work that must be removed.

parts.label: b

steps.text: Speed is greatest where resultant force is zero: $kx=mg$, so $x=0.025\,\mathrm{m}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Rolling from a known height
stem: A body of mass $M$ and radius $R$ rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp through height $h$. Its moment of inertia about its centre is $I=\beta MR^2$, where $\beta$ is a given positive constant. There are no dissipative losses.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A4 rolling without slip energy. Skill focus: rolling energy general inertia. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for its centre speed at the bottom.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare a hoop ($\beta=1$) and a solid sphere ($\beta=2/5$) released through equal heights.

steps.text: The sphere reaches a greater centre speed because a smaller fraction of the energy is rotational.

title: Clutching two coaxial rotors
stem: Rotor P has moment of inertia $0.30\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and rotates at $20\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Stationary rotor Q has inertia $0.20\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. A clutch couples them around their common fixed axis. External torque is negligible.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A4 coupling coaxial rotors. Skill focus: rotational collision energy loss. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find their final common angular speed.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the energy dissipated in the clutch.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the total angular momentum can be conserved while energy is dissipated.

steps.text: Clutch friction exerts internal equal and opposite torques, but transfers rotational kinetic energy into internal energy.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 proper length and simultaneous measurement. Skill focus: proper length definition. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: A
options.text: The separation measured in every frame without checking simultaneity.

options.label: B
options.text: The distance the rod travels during one second.

options.label: C
options.text: The separation of its ends measured in the rod’s rest frame.

options.label: D
options.text: The longest photograph of the moving rod.

steps.text: Option C. Proper length is measured in the rest frame of the object. In a moving frame, the endpoint positions used for a length measurement must be simultaneous in that frame.

title: One clock for two events

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 proper time and clock rate. Skill focus: proper time definition. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: A
options.text: The clock showing the longest interval in every frame.

options.label: B
options.text: A clock present at both events, so they occur at the same position in its rest frame.

options.label: C
options.text: Any pair of clocks at rest in any chosen frame.

steps.text: Option B. The proper time interval is measured by an inertial clock present at both events, whose spatial separation is zero in that clock’s frame. Arbitrarily separated clocks do not give this definition.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 invariant interval and causality. Skill focus: light spacetime interval. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: D

steps.text: Option A. For the light pulse, $|\Delta x|=c\Delta t$, so the squared terms cancel in every inertial frame.

steps.text: Option D. The proper interval is $4.0\,\mathrm{\mu s}$, so $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau=1.25(4.0)=5.0\,\mathrm{\mu s}$. This concerns emission events, not necessarily arrival times at a distant detector.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 simultaneity and clock synchronisation. Skill focus: relativity of simultaneity sign. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: A
options.text: The order depends only on their brightness.

options.label: D
options.text: They remain simultaneous in every frame.

steps.text: Option B. For right minus left, $\Delta t=0$ and $\Delta x>0$. Thus $\Delta t′=\gamma(\Delta t-v\Delta x/c^2)<0$: the right-hand event occurs earlier in S′.

subject: physics-hl

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 muon evidence in two frames. Skill focus: muon length contraction interpretation. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: The muon’s own lifetime is time-dilated in its rest frame.

options.label: D
options.text: The muon experiences no passage of time.

steps.text: Option A. In the muon rest frame its lifetime is the proper lifetime. The moving atmosphere is contracted along the motion, reducing the distance Earth travels to reach the muon.

title: Synchronising separated clocks
stem: Two clocks A and B are at rest $600\,\mathrm{m}$ apart in an inertial frame. A sends a light pulse when it reads $10.0\,\mathrm{\mu s}$. B immediately reflects the pulse; A receives it at $14.0\,\mathrm{\mu s}$. Use $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 simultaneity and clock synchronisation. Skill focus: Einstein clock synchronisation. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: What reading should B have at reflection under Einstein synchronisation?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Check consistency with the stated separation and explain whether a relatively moving frame agrees that the clocks are synchronised.

steps.text: Equal outward and return travel times place reflection halfway between the two A readings.
One-way travel time $600/c=2.00\,\mathrm{\mu s}$, consistent with the readings.
A moving frame generally does not assign simultaneous equal readings to separated clocks synchronised in this frame.

subject: physics-hl
title: Flashes at the ends of a moving rod
stem: A rod at rest in S has length $300\,\mathrm{m}$ along $x$. Its rear end at $x=0$ and front end at $x=300\,\mathrm{m}$ flash simultaneously at $t=0$. Frame S′ moves at $+0.80c$ relative to S. Use $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 simultaneity and clock synchronisation. Skill focus: simultaneity quantitative offset. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the time difference front minus rear in S′.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the spatial separation of these flash events in S′ and explain why it differs from the rod length measured in S′.

steps.text: $\Delta t′=-(5/3)(0.80)(300/c)=-1.33\,\mathrm{\mu s}$; the front flashes earlier.
The flash events are not simultaneous in S′, so their separation is not a length measurement.
The simultaneous S′ rod length is $L_0/\gamma=180\,\mathrm{m}$.

subject: physics-hl
title: Two station clocks and a passing spacecraft
stem: Stations A and B are at rest $6.0$ light-years apart in frame S. Their clocks are synchronised in S and both read zero at $t=0$. A spacecraft coasts from A towards B at $0.80c$. Its clock reads zero when it passes A at $t=0$. Ignore gravity. Frame S′ is the spacecraft rest frame, with its origin at this first passing event.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 simultaneity and clock synchronisation. Skill focus: inertial clock readings and simultaneity. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the reading on B’s clock and on the spacecraft clock when they pass one another.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the reading on B’s clock at the event on B’s worldline that is simultaneous in S′ with the spacecraft passing A.

steps.text: The S-frame travel time is $6.0/0.80=7.5\,\mathrm{years}$; this is the reading on B’s clock.
$\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-0.80^2}=5/3$; the spacecraft proper duration is $\Delta\tau=\Delta t/\gamma$.
Set $\Delta t′=\gamma(\Delta t-v\Delta x/c^2)=0$ with $\Delta x=6.0\,\mathrm{ly}$.
$\Delta t=v\Delta x/c^2=0.80(6.0)=4.8\,\mathrm{years}$. This is the B-clock reading, not the time when a light signal is received.

stem: Events A and B have $\Delta x=1200\,\mathrm{m}$ and $\Delta t=2.00\,\mathrm{\mu s}$ in S. Use $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 frames for special event separations. Skill focus: spacelike transformed separation. stem: At $t=0$ in a laboratory, a spacecraft at $x=0$ moves at $0.60c$ towards a stationary mirror at $x=300\,\mathrm{m}$. It emits a forward light pulse, which reflects and returns to the spacecraft. Use $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 transforming events and light paths. Skill focus: relativistic radar timing. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the laboratory time of reflection and of reception by the spacecraft.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the spacecraft-clock time between emission and reception and its radar distance $D=c\Delta\tau/2$.

title: Calibrating transformed axes
stem: A spacetime diagram for S uses coordinates $(x,ct)$ in light-seconds. A moving-frame time axis passes through P$(3,5)$; its spatial axis passes through Q$(5,3)$. The origins coincide. The axes of S have equal drawn scales.

verification.notes: Author checked physical assumptions, units, algebra and marking. Skill family: A5 worldlines and transformed axes. Skill focus: spacetime axes and Lorentz calibration. Equivalent correct forms accepted; no automatic error-carried-forward between unrelated parts. Numerical checks passed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the relative speed of S′ and S and the angle of the S′ time axis from the S time axis.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the S′ coordinates of P and Q.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a ruler measured along a slanted axis cannot simply use the S-axis tick spacing.

steps.text: The S′ origin has worldline $x=(v/c)ct$, so $v/c=3/5=0.60$.
Lorentz coordinates require calibrated ticks on transformed axes; their Euclidean lengths on the page are not coordinate values or spacetime intervals.
